          "h": "The theme: The acronym of Sodom (Se'udata d'David Malka), the Luz bone, Melaveh Malkah, and the departure of Shabbat. A holy master revealed that the letters of Sodom (S-D-M / סד״ם) form the acronym: Se'udata d'David Malka (סְעוּדָתָא דְּדָוִד מַלְכָּא / the festive post-Sabbath meal). The Luz bone in the spine—from which the body is resurrected and which never decomposes—derives nourishment solely from the Saturday night Melaveh Malkah meal. This meal carries the energy of eternal life; hence it is called the meal of King David who lives and endures forever, mirroring the banquet of the World to Come where David will recite the blessing over the preserved wine (Pesachim 119b). The Sabbath meal carries the taste of Manna, but only during the Sabbath itself; the Melaveh Malkah meal is like Isru Chag, binding the holiness of the Sabbath into the six secular workdays to sustain the food of angels. Angels are called \"standers\" (omedim) lacking free will; unable to ascend through effort, they cannot descend into sin, and without sin there is no death (Shabbat 55a). Mortality exists in mankind because of the sin of Adam and the instigation of the Serpent, which will be eradicated when Mashiach ben David slaughters the yetzer hara, elevating Israel above the angels. Shabbat is a \"good gift\" (matanah tovah, Shabbat 10b), fixed directly by Hashem; Yom Tov, sanctified by Israel through supernatural miracles, likewise becomes a fixed Sabbath where human labor ceases. Shabbat is Malkata (the Queen), the spiritual level of David HaMelech, channeling the glory of Hashem’s kingship into the lower worlds (\"in the light of the king's countenance is life\", Mishlei 16:15). During Shabbat, holiness is received temporarily; it becomes permanently engraved within the heart when the soul yearns after its departure, like disciples absorbing the wisdom of their master when he passes (Koheles Rabbah 12:11; shevak lan chayim). When Shabbat departs, the soul cries out: \"Woe, the additional soul is lost!\" (Beitzah 16a); through the Melaveh Malkah meal, this yearning anchors the Sabbath's holiness within the heart throughout the workdays."

        {
          "h": "The theme: The Shechinah in exile, the elevation of the night into day on Shabbat, and the feast of the Table (Se'udata d'David Malka). The Zohar at the end of Parashat Shelach states that the Shechinah never departs from Israel, even on secular weekdays. Shabbat Malkata—the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, and the resting of His Shechinah—conceals Herself with us throughout the exile and this world which is likened unto night. In the World to Come, which is likened unto day (Pesachim 2a), \"your Teacher shall not be hidden any more\" (Yeshayah 30:20), for all flesh will perceive the mouth of Hashem, which is the mystery of the Shechinah: \"Malkhut—Peh, Torah she-b'al Peh karinan lah\" (Patach Eliyahu). In the Future, the Oral Torah will reach consummate perfection in a day that is entirely Shabbat—neither day nor night (Zechariah 14:7)—for concerning Shabbat Scripture never writes \"and there was evening and there was morning\". The attribute of Night is the Oral Torah (\"there is no song of Torah save at night\", Shemos Rabbah 47:5), which Moshe studied by night and the Written Torah by day. The radiant illumination of the Oral Torah toiled over throughout the week shines on Shabbat, elevating the rung of Night to become a foretaste of the World to Come. In Tanna D'vei Eliyahu Rabbah (ch. 1) on \"the days that were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them\" (Tehillim 139:16): this is Shabbat, which unifies the six workdays into a single day without dark interruption, channeling its sanctity through the Melaveh Malkah meal (Se'udata d'David Malka). The crown of the Table (zer ha-shulchan) alludes to the Crown of Kingship (Keter Malkhut, Shemos Rabbah 34:2), for the table of a Jew is an altar before Hashem. All Israel are princes (Shabbat 128a) whom even the banquet of Solomon cannot suffice, for Avraham's feast was greater (Bava Metzia 83a). A se'udah sustains essential life, unlike a mishteh which seeks superfluous luxury; Solomon prayed \"feed me with my allotted bread\" (Mishlei 30:8), and Avraham's eating equaled seventy-four men (Masechet Sofrim 21:1), parallel to Yisro's feast before God (Shemos 18:12; Berachos 64a) where they derived pleasure from the radiance of the Shechinah—the bread of angels, the Torah of \"come, eat of my bread\" (Mishlei 9:5)."

          "h": "The theme: The giving of the Torah in Parashat Yisro, Yisro as head of proselytes, and the three divisions of human life. The Torah was given in the parashah named after Yisro to proclaim that the Crown of Torah lies open to all (Yoma 72b), given in the wilderness to declare it ownerless (hefker) to all inhabitants of the world (Mechilta, Bachodesh §1). Even a gentile convert who toils in Torah is equal to a High Priest (Bava Kamma 38a). Yisro was the premier proselyte who converted out of pure love of Torah; hence his descendants merited to sit in the Chamber of Hewn Stone (Lishkat HaGazit, Tanchuma, Yisro §4; I Divrei HaYamim 2:55). Yisro opened his home to feed Moshe, from whom Moshe derived his physical sustenance. Moshe’s vitality was the Torah named after him (\"Remember the law of Moses My servant\", Malachi 3:22). Intrinsically, Hashem bonds solely with Israel; yet because Israel lives among the nations, converts are drawn to join them. Moshe desired that the Torah expand to include sincere proselytes, and Hashem concurred: \"one law shall be unto him that is home-born, and unto the stranger\" (Shemos 12:49). Human life comprises three dimensions: that which is for oneself; that which is for the benefit of all creations (each soul tipping the scales of the universe, Kiddushin 40b); and that which is for the glory of Heaven (\"Hashem made all things for His purpose\", Mishlei 16:4; Yoma 38a). These correspond to the three names given to man: the name Hashem calls him (his unique divine purpose); the name father and mother call him (his service to fellow creations); and the name recorded in the book of his generations (his personal development, Midrash Tanchuma, Vayakhel §1; Midrash Shmuel 23). Moshe lived 120 years: forty years in Egypt completing his personal soul; forty years in Midian in Yisro's house serving other creations and extending holiness to proselytes; and forty years in the wilderness fulfilling his purpose before Hashem as redeemer, glorifying the Divine Name and teaching Torah to Israel (Sifrei, Devarim §357)."

          "h": "The theme: Self-love as love of Israel, the three crowns (Torah, Priesthood, Royalty), and the sacrifice of Chur. The three loves match the three dimensions of life. Love of Israel (Ahavat Yisrael) is intrinsic love of oneself, for all Israel constitutes a single collective body (\"you shall love your neighbor as yourself\", Vayikra 19:18). Authentic self-love exists only when one preserves spiritual wholeness; if a person stumbles into sin, the perfected soul detests the transgression within himself and within his fellow (\"those who love Hashem hate evil\", Tehillim 97:10; Pesachim 113a). This is the covenant of the oath (berit ha-alah, Devarim 29:11), preferring death to violating Hashem's will. The love of Torah serves all creations, for the Torah is the architectural blueprint of Creation (dimatria, Bereishis Rabbah 1:1). The love of Hashem completes the highest purpose: glorifying the Creator. The three crowns correspond to these three completions (Avos 4:13): the Crown of Torah belongs to the lovers of Torah, ownerless to all including converts, which Moshe acquired; the Crown of Priesthood belongs to those who serve Hashem in love, raising sweet fragrance to Him, which Aharon acquired; and the Crown of Royalty belongs to one who loves the nation and whom the nation loves. Originally, all Israel were destined to be a kingdom of priests and kings, as Korach argued (\"all the congregation are holy\", Bamidbar 16:3). Israel received two crowns at Sinai corresponding to Na'aseh and Nishma (Shabbat 88a), which were stripped because of the Golden Calf, preserved in the depths of their hearts until the Future. Aharon, who acted for the sake of Heaven during the Calf, acquired the priesthood of all Israel; Chur, who was martyred by the mob rebuking them out of supreme love of Israel, acquired the Crown of Royalty for his descendants through David, mirroring his mother Miriam (Puah) who risked her life to deliver Jewish infants from Pharaoh's decree (Shemos Rabbah 1:17)."

          "h": "The theme: Moshe as king and priest, why Torah is not an inheritance, Rabbi Akiva as the pillar of the Oral Law, and Yisro's feast with the elders. Moshe attained all perfections, serving as king in Jeshurun (Devarim 33:5) and as High Priest during the seven days of Consecration (Milu'im); yet royalty was not inherited by his sons. Although royalty issues from Torah (\"by me kings reign\", Mishlei 8:15), Moshe’s essence was the Torah itself, which cannot be inherited, being ownerless (hefker) to all. Hashem purposefully arranged that sons of Torah scholars do not routinely inherit scholarship (Nedarim 81a), lest mortals claim the Torah is a dynasty. Had Israel merited that Moshe enter the Holy Land, he would have completed the cosmic rectification, being the soul of Mashiach and eternal king. Proselytes are the \"surplus\" (yeter) in Israel (\"moreover the profit of the earth is in all\", Koheles 5:8). Rabbi Akiva—descended from converts (Gittin 57b)—beheld precious secrets that Moshe was not shown (Bamidbar Rabbah 19:6); yet Moshe's mind was put at ease when Rabbi Akiva attributed his insight as a \"Halachah to Moshe from Sinai\" (Menachos 29b), demonstrating that all is rooted in Moshe's transmission. Rabbi Akiva was the foundation of the Oral Torah: when the world was desolate, he established the southern disciples (Yevamos 62b) and formulated general principles and details (Yerushalmi Shekalim 5:1). He was born of converts because the love of Torah is revealed most brilliantly among proselytes: Israel was coerced at Sinai (\"holding the mountain over them like a cask\", Shabbat 88a), whereas the convert voluntarily abandons worldly comforts and licentiousness to bind himself to an afflicted, impoverished people. Coercion at Sinai applied to the Oral Torah which requires exhausting labor (Midrash Tanchuma, Noach §3); Hashem coerced Israel because inwardly their ancestral root yearns for Torah, like a recalcitrant husband who is coerced until he says \"I want to\" (Rambam, Hilchos Gezelah 1:9). Because converts display exemplary diligence in mitzvos (Pesachim 91b; Kiddushin 71a), Rabbi Akiva the son of converts became the foundation of the Oral Law. The Giving of the Torah was recorded in the portion of Yisro, the premier proselyte who abandoned royal wealth to trek into a barren wilderness. Yisro merited the feast of Torah scholars with Aharon (the Crown of Priesthood) and the elders of Israel (the Crown of Royalty), with Moshe standing to serve them, and Yisro embodying the Crown of Torah where the love of Torah is revealed at its peak!"

          "h": "The theme: Avraham Avinu acquiring all three crowns, his stature equaling seventy-four men, and the status of proselytes. Avraham Avinu merited all three crowns: Torah, Kingship, and Priesthood. His two kidneys welled with Torah like two flowing springs (Bereishis Rabbah 61:1, 95:3), inaugurating the two thousand years of Torah (Avodah Zarah 9a). Defeating the four kings, he acquired the Crown of Kingship when the nations crowned him in the Valley of the King (Bereishis Rabbah 43:5), foreshadowing King Mashiach. Priesthood was transferred from Shem (Melchizedek) to Avraham (\"You are a priest forever\", Tehillim 110:4; Nedarim 32b). Thus his stature, strength, and consumption equaled seventy-four men (Masechet Sofrim 21:1)—corresponding to Aharon, the seventy-two elders (including Eldad and Medad), and Yisro the father-in-law of Moshe. Avraham was the \"first of converts\" (Chagigah 3a), bearing the status of a proselyte until his circumcision, when he was promised the birth of Yitzchak. In Egypt, Israel endured exile corresponding to Avraham asking \"Whereby shall I know?\" (Bereishis 15:8)—a subtle flaw in faith (emunah). Until refined from the status of a proselyte to become an Ezrach (native-born), faith was not complete, requiring his descendants to be refined in Egypt (\"for your seed shall be a stranger\", ibid. 15:13), existing on the level of proselytes until entering the covenant at Sinai through circumcision, immersion, and sprinkling of blood."

          "h": "The theme: The souls of converts rooted in Parashat Yisro, Balaam's portion embracing Jewish transgressors, and Avraham's feast for the angels. All this was divine counsel to establish the entry of converts into Israel. Even a convert recites \"God of our fathers\" in prayer, invoking Avraham the \"father of many nations\" (Bikkurim 1:4). Yisro was included among the seventy-four men corresponding to Avraham, serving as the root of all proselytes. The souls of all converts are rooted in the opening of Parashat Yisro (Va-Yishma Yisro). Yisro and Balaam were present at Pharaoh's counsel against Israel (Sotah 11a): Yisro fled and became the root of proselytes; Balaam advised and was forced to prophesy Israel's greatness. Within Parashat Balak resides the spiritual root of Jewish apostates and heretics who forfeit their share in the World to Come, yet whose souls are preserved from total detachment (\"that no outcast be expelled from Him\", II Shmuel 14:14). The Dorshei Reshumot included all in the World to Come, but excluded Balaam because he was not of the seed of Israel. Avraham merited the Crown of Kingship and Priesthood through saving Sodom and Lot—rescuing the hidden soul of David and Mashiach. Sodom was the antithesis of hospitality; none of Avraham's converts among the heathen endured after his death (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer §29), wherefore Scripture records only his feast for the angels. Hosting guests is greater than receiving the Shechinah (Shabbat 127a). To the angels he said \"and sustain your heart\" (Bereishis 18:5)—a se'udah rather than a mishteh—because Avraham avoided luxuries. Though angels require no physical food, they derive spiritual sustenance: Rabbi Akiva taught that the Manna was the bread of angels (Yoma 75b). Mortals can weaken or strengthen the heavenly host (\"You have weakened the Rock that begot you\", Devarim 32:18; \"Ascribe strength unto God\", Tehillim 68:35; Zohar II, 32b). Avraham strengthened the heavenly retinue through hospitality; the angels absorbed his radiant lovingkindness, illuminating Lot in Sodom to host a feast and sparking the light of King David!"

          "h": "The theme: The primordial mention of a concept in the Torah, and the banquet of Lot revealing connections among the distant. Wherever a subject is mentioned for the first time in the Torah, there resides the concentrated essence and power of that concept. Thus the essential power of a banquet (mishteh) is rooted in Lot’s banquet. Although a feast generally serves as a medium of mutual fellowship, the paramount power of a mishteh lies in its ability to forge a connection where no natural affinity exists, awakening a deeply concealed spark. When wine enters, the hidden secret emerges (nichnas yayin yatza sod, Eruvin 65a), revealing an unexpected bond between polar opposites—uniting Lot (who was more excluded from the congregation of Hashem than all other nations) with holy angels of the highest sanctity!"

          "h": "The theme: The nations seeking assimilation with Israel, the feast of Ahasuerus, and \"worshipping idols in purity\". The ambition of the nations is to assimilate with Israel (\"Come, let us be one people\", Sanhedrin 39a), seeking that Israel not remain a distinct nation. Haman argued: \"There is a certain people scattered abroad and dispersed\" (Esther 3:8), the root of evil being the desire to mix good and evil together, tracing back to the Serpent defiling Chavah through the Tree of Knowledge (Da'as denoting intimacy). Ahasuerus hosted his feast because he calculated that the seventy years of Jeremiah's prophecy had expired without redemption (Megillah 11b), assuming Hashem had rejected Israel and that they would assimilate under his rule. He utilized the banquet to break down barriers. The Talmud calls attending a gentile feast \"worshipping idols in purity\" (Avodah Zarah 8a), even when eating kosher food served by Jewish attendants (Mordechai serving the Jews, Megillah 12a). In truth, a Jew's inner heart remains cleaved to Hashem (\"it is revealed and known before You that our will is to perform Your will\", Berachos 17a); at a feast the purity of the Jewish heart is demonstrated, their compliance being merely superficial (lifnim). Yet to the eyes of this world, sitting at a pagan banquet implies fellowship with the host who thanks his idols, attaching the name of idolatry to the guests. Because Israel bowed to the statue and attended the feast merely for outward appearance (lifnim), Hashem's decree of destruction was likewise merely superficial (lifnim, Megillah 12a). Ultimately, Israel was magnified physically through the fear of Mordechai, and spiritually by voluntarily re-accepting the entire Torah out of love (Shabbat 88a)!"

          "h": "The theme: The banquet of Esther breaking Haman, the altar table, and Nazir on Queen Esther. Haman boasted of being exclusively invited to Esther’s banquet (Esther 5:12), presuming he had attained union with her to the point of assaulting her upon the couch; this proved his undoing. Through wine, hidden secrets emerge: when inward affinity exists, a feast brings it forth; but where absolute division exists in the depths, wine exposes that total alienation. At Ahasuerus's banquet, while outward mingling appeared, the angels began to recall the merit of the Temple sacrifices (Megillah 12b). Every meal of Israel conducted in holiness mirrors sacrifices, for a Jew's table is an altar (Chagigah 27a); whereas the dining of the heathen is an offering to the dead (zivchei meitim) to fuel physical lust. Israel’s dining at the royal feast was termed \"idolatry in purity,\" avoiding forbidden foods and remaining free from lust. Mordechai and the Great Sanhedrin attended under imperial duress, exerting themselves to cleave unto Hashem. Their meals were accounted on High like sacrifices, awakening the merit of the Temple offerings. The righteous derived no pleasure from the feast of the wicked, for \"all the favors of the wicked are evil unto the righteous\" (Yevamos 103a; Nazir 23b), Esther deriving no pleasure from sin, accounted like the holy matriarchs!"

        {
          "h": "The theme: The yetzer hara pouncing through food and drink, the Well of Miriam, and turning the lament of wine into joy. The inception of all evil originates in the desire for food, beginning with the Tree of Knowledge. The yetzer hara pounces upon man solely through eating and drinking (Sifrei, Eikev §43; Berachos 32a); Iyov sacrificed offerings after his sons' banquets lest they sin (Iyov 1:5). Seduction operates primarily through wine: \"do not become intoxicated and you will not sin\" (Berachos 29b); the Tree of Knowledge was grapes which Chavah squeezed for Adam, wine causing his downfall (Sanhedrin 70a), and precipitating Noah’s disgrace after the Flood. Wine and sleep benefit the wicked by distracting them from harming others, but harm the righteous (Sanhedrin 71b), causing spiritual slumber and the slackening of hands from Torah. This was the sin of Israel and Haman's accusation: \"there is a people sleeping (yeshno) from the commandments\" (Megillah 13b). At Rephidim, Israel's hands slackened (rafu yedeihem), precipitating Amalek's assault; yet Hashem granted them the Well of Miriam (Be'era shel Miriam) tasting of wine and all celestial drinks (Devash LeFi), the beverage of ministering angels drawn from the wine preserved in its grapes. Every descent of Israel is for the sake of a higher ascent (yeridah l'tzorech aliyah); the slackening at Rephidim merited the Well of Miriam, the cure before the blow vanquishing Amalek. In Shushan, while Ahasuerus's wine brought wailing (yelalah) upon Vashti and Haman, for the Jews it became the gladdening wine of Torah (yayin ha-meshame'ach), where \"wine and fragrance make one wise\" (Yoma 76b), like pouring libations upon the altar when filling scholars' throats with wine (ibid. 71a)!"

All banquets of the seed of Israel are holy unto Hashem; even when one drinks ad d'lo yada until appearing externally like the gentiles, the mitzvah elevates the feast to holiness (\"Who has sanctified us with His commandments\"). \"The words of the Scribes are more beloved than the wine of the Torah\" (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:2), being secret mysteries revealed exclusively within the hearts of Israel. Conquering Amalek—who mimics Israel by displaying split hooves—is accomplished specifically through the Oral Torah. Therefore Yehoshua waged war against Amalek rather than Moshe: Moshe's face was like the sun (Bava Batra 75a), embodying the Written Torah; Yehoshua's face was like the moon, embodying the Oral Torah. Israel re-accepted the Oral Torah in the days of Esther (Shabbat 88a), over which the mountain had originally been held like a cask (Midrash Tanchuma, Noach §3). When wine enters the secret emerges (nichnas yayin yatza sod), revealing the secret embedded in Jewish hearts: the Holy One is the eternal heart of Israel (\"the rock of my heart and my portion forever\", Tehillim 73:26; Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2)!"

        {
          "h": "The theme: The eternal sanctity of Purim, the eschatological banquet of Leviathan and the Wild Ox, and the rectification of the Serpent's three vices. The Midrash on Mishlei (9:2) states that Purim will never be nullified, because its holiness foreshadows the World to Come. The Purim feast prefigures the banquet of the Future: in Midrash Esther Rabbah (2:4), Ahasuerus asked the Jews if their future reward would equal his banquet, and they answered: \"We have already eaten this in the days of Ahasuerus\". Although Ahasuerus spoke folly, his supernal Mazal perceived truth: the Great Sanhedrin purified themselves at that royal feast, bringing the cure before the blow and inaugurating the sanctity of Purim. The banquet of the Future will feature Leviathan, the Wild Ox (Shor HaBar), and the wine preserved in its grapes, attained by vanquishing the three destructive passions: Lust, Anger, and Arrogance (Avos 4:21). Ahasuerus's banquet combined all three: showing off his wealth (Arrogance), demanding Vashti (Lust), and burning with wrath (Anger). This mirrors the Serpent who began with arrogance (\"you shall be as gods\"), proceeded to lust (\"and the woman saw that the tree was good for food\"), and culminated in Cain's anger and murder (Esav's craft). Israel was chosen to rectify this Fall; the final rectification will occur in the World to Come, while in this world it is experienced through concealment on Purim. The feast of Purim is a foretaste of that future banquet, rectifying the forbidden eating of the Tree of Knowledge and Chavah's squeezing of the grapes!"

          "h": "The theme: Purim as the slaughter of the yetzer hara, assembling (kinus) of the righteous vs. the wicked, and linking the redemption of Adar to Nisan. On every Purim shines a sparkling of that celestial light of slaughtering the yetzer hara and rectifying the inception of the Fall. Therefore it is called days of \"feasting\" (mishteh)—an appellation given to no biblical festival, for festivals are times of gladness (zman simchah) rather than feasting, a banquet being inappropriate in an unredeemed world containing evil, save for the wicked for whom dispersion is beneficial. While an unholy banquet fosters division, the gathering of the righteous (kinus la-tzaddikim) brings true fellowship: assembling generates the holy feast, just as the brothers reunited with Yosef before drinking wine, and the Jews assembled to defend themselves in the days of Mordechai and Esther. Through this holy fellowship, Mishlo'ach Manot, and Matanot LaEvyonim, Israel merits to taste the banquet of the Future: the eradication of the yetzer hara from the heart regarding the three cardinal sins (Idolatry, Immorality, Bloodshed) that destroyed the First Temple, and baseless hatred (sin'at chinam) that destroyed the Second Temple. At the beginning of the Second Temple, the Sages sought to rectify this discord; \"he that is of a merry heart has a continual feast\" (Mishlei 15:15). Just as Isru Chag binds a festival to the year, and Melaveh Malkah binds Shabbat to the weekdays, extending the Purim feast into the night anchors the sanctity of Purim throughout the entire year, meriting to link the redemption of Purim to the ultimate redemption of Nisan!"

        {
          "h": "The theme: Why the Megillah begins and ends with the might of Ahasuerus, open miracles vs. natural garments, and the future status of Purim as a Yom Tov. The Talmud records: \"He who reads the Megillah must read all of it, from the might of Ahasuerus\" (Megillah 19a), and this is the binding halachic ruling. The Megillah makes this its cornerstone by opening with the 180-day feast of Ahasuerus and closing with: \"And the king Ahasuerus laid a tribute... and all the acts of his power and of his might\" (Esther 10:1–2). In every sacred book, the beginning and the end encapsulate the entire message. Superficially, the tax tribute seems extraneous to the miracle; yet every biblical miracle establishes an enduring imprint of holiness within the soul. The biblical festivals were accompanied by overt supernatural miracles breaking the laws of nature. On Purim, however, \"we are still the servants of Ahasuerus\" (Megillah 14b); the miracle was veiled within the natural order (derech ha-teva), enacted through Esther’s intercession. The holiness of Purim was initiated by Israel below, confirmed by Heaven: \"they confirmed Above what was accepted below\" (Megillah 7a)—mirroring the Oral Torah where rabbinic novellae express the words of the Living God. Because it was born of human initiative, Israel did not accept Purim as a work-prohibited festival (Yom Tov). Esther was composed through the Holy Spirit (Megillah 7a); seeing it confirmed Above, the Sages initially thought to make it a full festival, but Israel perceived that in this world human effort (hishtadlut) is required. Like a lost object found after exhausting toil (yagati u-matzati, Megillah 6b), Israel attained deliverance through prayers, fasting, and military struggle against their enemies. The rest they attained (ve-no'ach) prefigures the future; when the seed of Amalek is eradicated completely, Purim will become a full Yom Tov as originally envisioned!"

Similarly, if he says to you: I have not labored but nevertheless I have found success, do not believe him. If, however, he says to you: I have labored and I have found success, believe him. The Gemara comments: This applies only to matters of Torah, as success with respect to Torah study is in accordance with the toil and effort invested. But with regard to success in business, it all depends upon assistance from Heaven, as there is no correlation between success and effort. And even with regard to matters of Torah, we said this only with regard to sharpening one’s understanding of Torah, as the more one labors, the deeper the understanding of the material he achieves.…’"

          "h": "The theme: Rebbe planting on Purim, Ahasuerus and Nebuchadnezzar as \"the Head\" of the husk, and David establishing the eternal Temple. Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi planted saplings on Purim, sought to abolish Tisha B'Av when it fell on Shabbat, and bathed on the Seventeenth of Tammuz (Megillah 5b). The Gemara links these by stating: \"Ahasuerus is the brother of the Head and his counterpart: the one killed and destroyed, and the other sought to destroy\" (Megillah 11a). Nebuchadnezzar was the \"head of gold\" (reisha d'dahava, Daniel 2:38; Sanhedrin 107a), standing in the unholy husk opposite King David in holiness. King Solomon built the physical Temple, but Scripture attributes its eternal foundation to David (\"a song at the dedication of the house of David\", Tehillim 30:1), for the gates sunk into the earth were never dominated by enemies (Sotah 9a). David purchased the Temple Mount and consecrated it with an eternal holiness that was never nullified (kidsha l'sha'ata v'kidsha l'atid lavo). The subterranean drainage channels (shitin) he excavated were never destroyed. Scripture only designates an enduring structure as a \"house,\" wherefore the Temple is attributed to David who consecrated it like Yaakov (\"Bet-El\"). Physical buildings constructed by Solomon were destroyed, leaving merely the written account; Solomon declared: \"and this was my portion of all my labor\" (Koheles 2:10)—pointing with his finger unto his inner holy yearning which alone endures. The heart of kingship is concealed; David is the root of the moon's light (\"David king of Israel lives and endures\", Rosh Hashanah 25a), whose core light receives from the sun eternally even when eclipsed to earth. When David ascended to \"the head where he bowed himself unto God\" (II Shmuel 15:32)—the lookout (Tzofim) overlooking the sanctuary—holy awe seized him, bowing spontaneously without conscious effort (Yerushalmi Berachos 2:4). This summit is \"the secret of Hashem is to them that fear Him\" (Tehillim 25:14). Yet in this world, every fruit is encased in a husk of sackcloth (meshcha d'chivya), where the \"Head\" denotes the manifest husk."

          "h": "The theme: David fleeing from Absalom, the dread of Chillul Hashem, and the captive woman (Yefat To'ar). When David fled from Absalom, he feared his eternal dynasty was lost, and that a king who is the Head of Royalty would be slain by his own son, causing a catastrophic desecration of the Divine Name (Chillul Hashem). Hashem's Name is His earthly sovereignty (Malkhut); the gravest sin in the world—atoned fully only through death—is Chillul Hashem (Yoma 86a), which severs the connection between man and God. David was born to rectify Adam's sin and attain eternal life (\"he asked life of You, and You gave it him\", Tehillim 21:5; Sanhedrin 107a). When David saw Absalom rebelling to kill him, he thought it were better to worship idols secretly in order to absorb the blow within the unholy husk rather than allow a holy king to be murdered by his son. Hushai the Archite challenged him: \"Shall a king like you worship idols?!\" (Sanhedrin 107a), for David had slain his yetzer hara, his heart being a void. David replied: \"Shall a king like me be slain by his own son?!\" A living creature reproduces its likeness—a man does not father a beast—and if his own son was wicked, David feared he still retained an unrectified root of evil. Yaakov, whose bed was whole, never died, for \"from a good lion no bad cub issues\"; likewise Hashem promised David an eternal covenant where his seed will never be severed (II Shmuel 7:14–16; Yirmiyah 33:20–26). When David saw Absalom seeking his life, he feared the husk of the Serpent had not been removed from him; Hushai answered: \"Why did you marry the beautiful captive woman (Yefat To'ar)?\" (Sanhedrin 107a)—explaining that Absalom's corruption derived not from David's holy seed, but from his mother Maachah!"

          "h": "The theme: David's consummate holiness versus Nebuchadnezzar's absolute corruption, the destruction of the Temple, and Nebuchadnezzar as the essential sinner. Just as King David in holiness was completely whole without any defect, so Nebuchadnezzar within the unholy husk (kelipah) was in absolute corruption, to the extent that no rectification could ever emerge from his seed, his essence having become entirely evil without any admixture of good. Thus from a good lion no bad cub issues, while from Nebuchadnezzar no good cub could emerge (Sanhedrin 96b on Yirmiyah 51:9: \"We would have healed Babylon, but she is not healed\", because he destroyed the Holy Temple). King David completely separated the evil husk of the Primordial Man from his soul, leaving himself entirely good and the evil entirely evil. The destruction of the Temple—coming to forcefully banish and remove the resting of the Shechinah from the lower worlds—flowed from absolute evil devoid of any goodness. Concerning this the Midrash states on Koheles 9:2: \"'as is the good'—this is David; 'as is the sinner'—this is Nebuchadnezzar\". Throughout Scripture, a \"sin\" (chet) denotes an unintentional transgression (shogeg), matching Bava Metzia (33b) where an unlearned person's intentional sins are accounted as unintentional errors. Nebuchadnezzar was the polar opposite of the wisdom of the Oral Torah, which is Israel's perception to serve their Father in Heaven; possessing not a single drop or fragrance of this wisdom, he is designated \"the sinner\" as a proper essential noun, his entire essence being sin!"

        {
          "h": "The theme: Ahasuerus opposite Solomon, sitting on the royal throne, and the unholy heart (lev ha-tamei). Ahasuerus is called the \"brother of the Head\" (Megillah 11a) because he was the husk standing opposite the holiness of King Solomon. Targum Sheni on Esther 1:2 (\"when the king sat on the throne of his kingdom\") states that Ahasuerus sought to sit upon the golden throne of Solomon; according to Targum Rishon and Midrash Esther Rabbah (1:12), when he was unable to sit upon Solomon's actual throne, he constructed his own throne in its exact likeness. Scripture hints at this likeness, for Ahasuerus presumed he possessed affinity to Solomon, being the surrounding unholy husk opposite Solomon's holiness. Yet the rod of wickedness cannot rest upon the lot of the righteous (Tehillim 125:3). King David was the true builder of the eternal Temple and the true sustainer of Israel, fighting their battles; David is the head of all kings whose monarchy endures forever, as \"my servant David shall be their prince forever\" (Yechezkel 37:25). In Solomon’s reign, all this expanded with greater splendor in the construction of the Temple, and the nation flourished: \"Judah and Israel were many... eating and drinking and making merry\" (I Melachim 4:20)—prefiguring the World to Come (\"Behold, My servants shall eat... behold, My servants shall drink\", Yeshayah 65:13). Like Shabbat and Yom Tov where human toil ceases, Solomon's reign represented the reward following spiritual labor, sitting upon the throne of Hashem (I Divrei HaYamim 29:23) in the perfected image of God like Adam before the Fall. Yet that perfection was temporary; Scripture notes: \"And Solomon loved Hashem, to walk in the statutes of David\" (I Melachim 3:3)—denoting a holy yearning to walk like David, rather than actualized permanent attainment. In parallel opposition stood Ahasuerus, seeking to destroy all things, the antithesis of Solomon. Nebuchadnezzar was the unholy skull (gulgalta), while Ahasuerus was the unholy heart (lev ha-tamei) whose root is haughtiness, mirroring the primordial kings who died through arrogance thinking \"I shall reign\" (Zohar; Mishlei 16:5)!"

        {
          "h": "The theme: The threefold boasting (wisdom, might, riches), Solomon's peaceful conquest, and Ahasuerus's banquet mimicking life. Pride and boasting center upon three attributes: wisdom, might, and riches: \"Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches; but let him that glories glory in this, that he understands and knows Me\" (Yirmiyah 9:22–23). When used to know Hashem, these attributes are praiseworthy (\"a woman that fears Hashem, she shall be praised\", Mishlei 31:30); otherwise they are falsehood and vanity. King Solomon was blessed with all three. His primary request was wisdom to fear Hashem and know Him, which is the hallmark of Kingship (\"a king when he bows does not straighten until finishing the prayer\", Berachos 34b). Hashem granted him riches and honor in place of the lives of his enemies which he did not ask (I Melachim 3:11–13). Solomon was a \"man of rest\" (ish menuchot, I Divrei HaYamim 22:9), his era being one of peace and quiet from all foes; his might did not consist of military warfare, but of honor whereby all nations spontaneously submitted to his rule (\"for he had dominion over all... and he had peace on all sides\", I Melachim 5:4). There are two modes of subduing the yetzer: subjugation (lachpaya) and transformation (l'hafcha). David subdued the yetzer through warfare and fasting (Tehillim 109:22; Bava Batra 17a), all fearing him; whereas Solomon enjoyed the pleasures of this world in holiness with the knowledge that God will bring everything into judgment (Koheles 2:10, 11:9), transforming the bitter into sweet (l'hafcha) like the sacred delight of Shabbat. In counterpoint, the unholy harlot (eshet zenunim) mimics holiness like an ape before man. Ahasuerus hosted his feast of eating, drinking, and rejoicing, showing off his riches and honor in peace without war; but lacking the primary crown of wisdom, he was a foolish king (melech tipeish), his worldly cleverness being true folly before Hashem!"

                      "text": ": ‘The verse states: “And when these days were fulfilled, the king made a feast for all the people that were present in Shushan the capital” (Esther 1:5). Rav and Shmuel disagreed as to whether this was a wise decision. One said: Ahasuerus arranged a feast for the residents of Shushan, the capital, after the feast for foreign dignitaries that preceded it, as mentioned in the earlier verses, indicating that he was a clever king. And the other one said: It is precisely this that indicates that he was a foolish king. The one who said that this proves that he was a clever king maintains that he acted well when he first brought close those more distant subjects by inviting them to the earlier celebration, as he could appease the residents of his own city whenever he wished.…’"

        {
          "h": "The theme: Lower wisdom (Chokhmah Tata'ah) rooted in heart's yearning, gentile wisdom versus Torah, and Solomon's foreign wives. All wisdom on man's part (Chokhmah Tata'ah) is essentially the yearning (cheshek) to acquire wisdom; Hashem gives wisdom unto the wise (Daniel 2:21) who already possess this initial yearning. Solomon’s wisdom matched his boundless desire: \"and all Solomon's desire (cheshek Shlomo) which he was pleased to build\" (I Melachim 9:19)—this holy desire enduring forever in his three sacred books (Mishlei, Koheles, Shir HaShirim). True lower wisdom resides in a heart filled with the fear of Heaven; without fear, \"Wherefore is there a price in the hand of a fool to get wisdom, seeing he has no heart to it?\" (Mishlei 17:16; Yoma 72b). A blessing is recited over gentile philosophers: \"Who has given of His wisdom unto flesh and blood\" (Berachos 58a), but not \"unto them that fear Him\". Gentile intellect is merely a price in the hand of a fool; when an idolater speaks a wise saying (Megillah 16a), it is a temporary gift from Hashem, but his essence remains foolish because he lacks truth, which belongs to Yaakov. Scripture never attributes wisdom to Ahasuerus, for true wisdom is divine. Ahasuerus boasted of his riches and honor, which have an external parallel to Solomon's temporal wealth. Solomon absorbed these worldly pleasures from the gentile kings he conquered through peace; he married foreign princesses thinking he could rectify the entire world so that evil cease entirely, fulfilling: \"the wolf shall dwell with the lamb\" (Yeshayah 11:6)—the lamb being Israel among seventy wolves (Midrash Tanchuma, Toldot §5). But Israel endures among the wolves only by remaining apart (\"a people that dwells alone\", Bamidbar 23:9); intermarriage destroys the root of Judaism, drawing forward the foreskin (Eruvin 19a) like a dog that cannot be detached (Midrash Tanchuma, Vayeshev §8). Solomon thought he could elevate all worldly lusts into holiness through transformation (l'hafcha); but the time for universal rectification had not arrived, and his foreign wives turned his heart (I Melachim 11:4). While they wrought no change in his inner heart, they introduced a subtle leaning toward unrectified evil, which ultimately generated the imperial might of Ahasuerus!"

        {
          "h": "The theme: Israel partaking in the feast of Ahasuerus for the sake of Heaven, extracting the holy spark, and Esther clothing herself in the Holy Spirit. Israel during that generation—including Mordechai the Righteous—partook of the feast of that wicked one. They enjoyed the varied pleasures of the banquet, for Ahasuerus asked them if such delights exist in the World to Come (Midrash Esther Rabbah 2:4). In truth, their inward intention was in absolute holiness for the sake of Heaven, seeking to extract the swallowed sparks of holiness from the mouth of the unholy husk, acting merely for outward appearance (lifnim, Megillah 12a). To the righteous, worldly indulgence under duress is experienced without bodily pleasure, as Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi testified that he derived no physical pleasure from this world (Kesubos 104a), and Hillel viewed sustaining his physical frame merely as bestowing kindness upon an impoverished guest in his house (Vayikra Rabbah 34:3). Ahasuerus sought to mimic King Solomon like an ape before man; Israel attended the feast to rectify this mimicry, proving that within Israel worldly pleasure remains sanctified. Through this they prepared the cure before the blow: Esther entering unto the king, which resembled taking an Aramean woman (which zealots may punish, Sanhedrin 82a; Mordechai on Yevamos), where cohabitation with an uncircumcised pagan binds the woman to him (Bereishis Rabbah 80:11). Yet Esther sanctified herself so that no unholy attachment adhered to her. When she approached the inner court, \"she put on royal apparel\" (va-tilbash malchut, Esther 5:1)—which the Sages expounded: she clothed herself in the Holy Spirit (Megillah 15a), separating from all physical worldly pleasure. Sanctity exists exclusively where there is a fence against sexual immorality (geder ervah, Vayikra Rabbah 24:6); the Holy Spirit cannot rest where there is the slightest leaning toward carnal defilement, particularly attaching unto an uncircumcised, impure body. Esther clothed herself in the Kingdom of Heaven (Malkhut Shamayim)—like Solomon sitting upon the throne of Hashem—which is the manifestation of the Shechinah in the lower worlds. When Israel was exiled to Elam, the Shechinah accompanied them: \"And I will set My throne in Elam\" (Yirmiyah 49:38; Yerushalmi Ta'anit 1:3), destroying Vashti, Haman, and his sons (Megillah 10b). In exile the Shechinah clothes Herself in the dark sackcloth of the husk (levush sak d'kelipah), but Esther was crowned to reign alongside the emperor, clothed with royal authority to annul the unholy Persian decrees. The kings' hearts are in the hand of Hashem (Mishlei 21:1); the redemption began when Esther put on royalty, standing so fearless before Ahasuerus that when she denounced \"an adversary and enemy\" (Esther 7:6) she initially pointed toward Ahasuerus himself (Megillah 16a), knowing imperial authority was stripped from him and granted unto her!"

        {
          "h": "The theme: The Sages attending the feast to extract holy sparks, the prison of forbidden foods, and Solomon's three prohibitions. The Sages in Shushan attended the feast aware that gentile banquets are termed offerings to the dead (zivchei meitim, Avodah Zarah 8a). Every food that sustains human life contains holy sparks (nitzotzot kedoshim) through which man lives (\"and You preserve them all\", Nechemyah 9:6). Even forbidden foods contain a holy spark sustaining them, but that spark is locked in a dark prison (beit ha-asurim) from which mortal man cannot extract it, wherefore its consumption is forbidden until the Future when Hashem \"looses the prisoners\" (Tehillim 146:7) at the banquet of Leviathan. Only accidentally through nullification in a mixture (bitul) can an unholy mixture return to permissibility without human intention, for no mortal may intentionally nullify a prohibition. An accidental stumbling in eating is a deep mystery directed by the Master of Causes for the benefit of creatures, yet it never occurs through great early pious masters (Chullin 5b). Gentile offerings to the dead lack spiritual life and cannot be nullified even in any minute quantity (kol shehu), their ash being forbidden like buried corpses; at the Resurrection they will not rise, but will be destroyed when death is swallowed up forever. The Sages attended under duress, knowing it was not one of the cardinal sins requiring martyrdom; they deduced that divine providence orchestrated their attendance to extract holy sparks swallowed by Ahasuerus belonging to the soul of King Solomon. Solomon sought to outsmart the Torah regarding the three prohibitions of a king: not multiplying silver and gold (wealth), horses (might), or wives (wisdom), claiming \"I will multiply and not turn aside\" (Sanhedrin 21b). Solomon knew his wealth belonged to Hashem, asking only for his apportioned bread (Mishlei 30:8); his expansive heart utilized all wealth for the glory of Hashem, which has no boundary. Multiplying horses stems from Egypt—the root of relying upon human might and enslavement (\"who is Hashem that I should obey His voice?\"). The Exodus taught Israel to rely upon Hashem alone (\"and we will not ride upon horses, neither will we say any more to the work of our hands: You are our gods\", Hoshea 14:4). Solomon believed his royal power would never return the people to Egyptian self-reliance, his words infusing faith into Jewish hearts!"

          "h": "The theme: The warning against multiplying wives, Egyptian wisdom, might, and riches, and the fatal flaw of Solomon's foreign marriages. The Torah commanded: \"Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away\" (Devarim 17:17). Solomon assumed that his infinite breadth of heart could never be swayed; yet even wisdom has boundaries: \"Have you found honey? eat so much as is sufficient for you, lest you be filled therewith, and vomit it\" (Mishlei 25:16; Chagigah 13a; Koheles 7:16). Seeking to outsmart the Torah, he vomited it, expounded in Shemos Rabbah (6:1) on \"Agur ben Yakeh\" (Mishlei 30:1)—who gathered (agar) and vomited (heki). Hashem showed him that not a single letter of the Torah can be nullified (Sanhedrin 21b). Solomon’s intention was for Heaven: to rectify the entire universe through his wisdom, thinking he would turn their hearts to holiness. Egypt possessed unholy counterparts to wisdom, might, and riches: Solomon excelled past the wisdom of Egypt (I Melachim 5:10); Egypt amassed the world's wealth during the famine under Yosef (Pesachim 87b). Opposite the holy land where \"the people is strong\" (Bamidbar 13:28) and five pursue a hundred through Torah (Vayikra 26:8), Egypt cultivated these powers in the unholy husk. Solomon married Pharaoh’s daughter thinking he could elevate these unholy sparks into holiness. A prophet may suspend a commandment temporarily for the glory of Heaven (\"it is time for Hashem to act, they have made void Your law\", Tehillim 119:126), but never regarding idolatry (Sanhedrin 90a). Idolatry is called \"dead\" (meitim), having no holy sparks. Solomon thought he could infuse life into the dead through the dew of Torah (Kesubos 111b). Pharaoh sent Solomon workmen destined to die that year (Bamidbar Rabbah 19:3; Tanchuma, Chukat §6), hinting that Egypt possessed only death, but Solomon failed to heed the sign. There were sparks of holiness in Pharaoh’s daughter and his foreign wives, but they were submerged in the deepest abyss of evil, eating unripe fruit (paga) like David with Batsheva (Sanhedrin 107a). Because they were unsuited for him, ruin resulted: on the day Solomon married Pharaoh’s daughter, the destruction of the Temple was decreed: \"For this city has been to Me as a provocation of Mine anger and of My fury\" (Yirmiyah 32:31; Vayikra Rabbah 12:5)!"

          "h": "The theme: Mordechai and the Sanhedrin attending the feast as a transgression for the sake of Heaven (aveirah lishmah), the eradication of the house of Nebuchadnezzar through Vashti's death, and Solomon completing the revelation of David. Seeing that the seventy years of Babylonian exile had concluded without redemption, Mordechai and the Sages reasoned that Heaven orchestrated Ahasuerus's banquet to allow them to rectify the sin of King Solomon and achieve the final redemption. Every rectification is enacted within the very arena of the original fall when conducted in holiness. Although Israel should have mourned over the exile and the display of Persian glory opposite the royalty of Solomon, they attended under compulsion, intending their participation for the sake of Heaven as an aveirah lishmah. In every aveirah lishmah, while the deed itself requires expiation and retribution (as Tosafos writes in Bava Kamma 91b regarding fasting for an unnecessary fast), the pure intention receives reward as a mitzvah not for its own sake (mitzvah she-lo lishmah). The reward was the immediate salvation achieved through the execution of Vashti—the sole surviving descendant of Nebuchadnezzar (\"neither name, nor remnant, nor son, nor grandson\", Yeshayah 14:22; Megillah 10b)—eradicating the house of Babylon and destroying the unholy husk standing opposite King David. David was \"alive and enduring\" (Rosh Hashanah 25a), but the revelation of his personal rectification for Batsheva remained concealed until Solomon built the Temple. David and Solomon are the brain and the heart (Mocha and Liba, two inseparable companions), the brain representing concealed thought (the letter Yud) and the heart representing outward expansion into active deed (the letter Hei). Solomon actualized David's potential; when the Ark entered the Holy of Holies, the gates opened and all witnessed that David was forgiven (Shabbat 30a). Had Solomon preserved his heart like David, he would have attained true length of days in the World to Come (Chullin 142a), an eternal Temple, and the final redemption. But when Solomon sinned, the Temple was destroyed, concealing David's achievements and giving rise to Nebuchadnezzar. Nebuchadnezzar descended from Solomon through the Queen of Sheba (Rashi on I Melachim 10:13), for intermarriage conceals the holy covenant (Yesod). Yaakov Avinu, whose bed was whole because he never experienced nocturnal emission (Yevamos 76a), established an eternal seed where even an uncircumcised Jew is legally called circumcised (Nedarim 31b); worldly sins are merely thorns surrounding the myrtle!"

        {
          "h": "The theme: King David raising the yoke of repentance, Jeconiah's decree overturned through the Great Sanhedrin, and Semiramis taking the kingdom. David raised the yoke of repentance (Avodah Zarah 5a), rectifying all blemishes through the Book of Psalms to cut down the thorns encircling the celestial rose. Like Yaakov who never died (Ta'anit 5b), David is alive and enduring; physical death entered the world through Adam's 130 years of impurity (Eruvin 18b), which David and Mashiach rectify. David tasted the Tree of Life (\"he asked life of You, and You gave it him\", Tehillim 21:5). Whoever rectifies the covenant completely—whether through sinless purity like Yaakov and Eliyahu or consummate repentance like David—is promised that his seed will endure forever (\"his seed shall endure forever\", Tehillim 89:37). Yet when Nebuchadnezzar's power arose, exiling Jeconiah (Yechonyah) and the craftsmen, the decree was issued: \"Write you this man childless\" (Yirmiyah 22:30), threatening to extinguish the Davidic dynasty. The Great Sanhedrin placated Nebuchadnezzar's queen, Semiramis (Vayikra Rabbah 19:6; Esther Rabbah 3:2), who persuaded the emperor to allow Jeconiah's wife into the dungeon. This was the true taking of royalty (natlu malchut) by Semiramis: overriding Nebuchadnezzar to preserve the Davidic seed and destroy his memory! In the dungeon, Jeconiah's wife saw blood and he separated from her, rectifying his past sins of cohabiting during impurity (niddah, which carries the penalty of childlessness, Vayikra 20:21). Through this self-restraint the monarchy of David was rebuilt. The decree was worded \"Write you this man childless\"—commanded to be written in Jeremiah to record human consequence and the majesty of repentance, paving the way for the destruction of the house of Nebuchadnezzar!"

          "h": "The theme: Esther rectifying Solomon's foreign wives, the Oral Torah expanding from the Great Assembly, and conquering Amalek before rest (be-hani'ach). There remained the unholy side opposing King Solomon, which Esther arose to rectify through a transgression for the sake of Heaven (aveirah lishmah), entering the mixture of human seed and bestial seed from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. Da'as denotes union (\"and Adam knew Eve\", Bereishis 4:1); Solomon sought to transform the Tree of Knowledge into the Tree of Life, and the Sages in Shushan and Esther succeeded in this. Through the miracle of Esther, Israel re-accepted the Torah out of love—the Tree of Life (Eitz HaChayim, Tanna D'vei Eliyahu Rabbah ch. 1). Then began the revelation of the Oral Torah through the Men of the Great Assembly, who taught: \"raise up many disciples\" (transmitting the Oral Law from master to student) and \"make a fence around the Torah\" (enacting rabbinic hedges). During the prophetic era, Israel sought prophecy (bnei ha-nevi'im); from the Great Assembly onward, all Israel sought wisdom in the Oral Torah (talmidei chachamim), completing Kingship. This began after the eradication of Amalek in the days of Haman, for Amalek causes the slackening of hands from Torah (attacking at Rephidim, Bechorot 5b). When the voice is not the voice of Jacob in synagogues and study halls, the hands are the hands of Esav (Bereishis Rabbah 65:20); the Oral Torah requires exhausting labor (Tanchuma, Noach §3), over which the mountain had been coerced as a cask. In Ahasuerus's days they re-accepted the Oral Torah out of love, toiling without fatigue having blotted out Amalek's coldness. The command to blot out Amalek applies after appointing a king and when Hashem grants rest (be-hani'ach, Devarim 25:19). Establishing a king is establishing the Oral Torah; yet during rest (hani'ach), when a person seeks ease, the Torah warns not to cast off the yoke of divine service to pursue personal desires, for that is true servitude to the yetzer. One who accepts the yoke of Torah is freed from the yoke of government and worldly toil (Avos 3:5; Sanhedrin 99b); man is born to toil in Torah, placing upon himself the yoke like an ox to the plow (Avodah Zarah 5b). King Saul, whose monarchy was borrowed, failed to destroy Agag; his descendants Mordechai and Esther finished the task, establishing the eternal monarchy of the House of David!"

          "h": "The theme: Why Purim was not established as a full Yom Tov, Darius building the Second Temple, and the failure of the Second Return through foreign marriages. The Sages initially thought to establish Purim as a work-prohibited festival (Yom Tov), believing they had completely blotted out the seed of Amalek from the world. Had this occurred, the final redemption would have arrived; but Israel remained \"the servants of Ahasuerus\" (Megillah 14b), the Divine Name and Throne remaining incomplete. Witnessing the government entrusted unto Esther and Mordechai, they assumed they were subjects of Esther who clothed herself in the Kingdom of Heaven. Yet the generation of Israel—the \"children of prophets\"—refused to accept Purim as a Yom Tov, for despite the great salvation, building the Second Temple was denied unto Esther (Ahasuerus granting her \"unto half the kingdom\"—excluding the Temple that stood in the middle, Megillah 15b). The Temple was rebuilt decades later by her son Darius. Although Darius was halachically pure from his mother (a child of a Jewish mother and gentile father being kosher, Kiddushin 68b), he was born of the demon-counterpart (sheidah, Etz Chayim, Sha'ar Kelipat Nogah ch. 6; Arba Me'ot Shekel Kesef 82a) which Esther separated from her holy essence. Had the mixture of the Tree of Knowledge been completely rectified, all evil would have vanished, Ahasuerus's memory would have perished like Nebuchadnezzar's, and Esther would have married Zerubbabel the governor of Judah to reign over the entire earth! Israel was worthy of miracles in the days of Ezra like the days of Joshua (Berachos 4a); had they ascended en masse as in the First Commonwealth, the redemption would have been eternal like silver that never rots (Yoma 9b; Yerushalmi). But sin prevented this: the men of the Second Temple intermarried with foreign women (Zohar II, 7a), causing the blemish to return. Esther's union was under duress as an aveirah lishmah rectifying Solomon; their marriages were willful transgressions. Because the final rectification was not achieved, Purim was not accepted as a full Yom Tov!"

          "h": "The theme: The custom of refraining from work on Purim, the expansion of the Oral Law after the Destruction, and Rabbi Akiva's comprehensive vision. Although strictly speaking Purim was not established as a full festival prohibiting labor, the Jewish people adopted a widespread customary restriction against work (Megillah 5b) in order not to be distracted from the joyful obligations of feasting and merrymaking. This custom likely originated following the destruction of the Temple, when the Sages intensified their spiritual efforts in establishing the Oral Torah (Torah she-b'al Peh). This effort culminated with Rabbi Akiva, who structured general principles and specific details (Yerushalmi Shekalim 5:1), perceiving profound secrets that even Moshe Rabbeinu was not explicitly shown in his generation (Bamidbar Rabbah 19:6). As Koheles Rabbah expounds on \"the words of the wise are as goads\" (Koheles 12:11): when are their teachings most firmly planted? When their masters are gathered from the world. With the destruction of the Temple—the very wellspring of wisdom drawn through the Holy Spirit—the remaining few scholars exerted extraordinary labor in Torah study, meriting unprecedented revelations and reinforcing the celebration of Purim, whose core joy commemorates the voluntary re-acceptance of the Oral Torah out of love."

        {
          "h": "The theme: Rebbe compiling the Mishnah, his planting on Purim, and the distinction between the servitude of Pharaoh and the ongoing servitude of Ahasuerus. Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi (Rebbe) concluded the era of the Tannaim, compiling the Mishnah which serves as the foundational text of the entire Oral Law, hinting at every future insight. Rebbe descended from King David; his compilation aimed to establish the spiritual stature of Kingship (Malkhut), bringing about the ingathering of the exiles through the study of the Mishnayot (Vayikra Rabbah 7:2 on Hoshea 8:10). Rebbe was worthy of being Mashiach had his generation merited (Sanhedrin 98b), remaining \"alive and enduring\" even after his physical death (Kesubos 103a). Rebbe planted joyous saplings on Purim (Megillah 5b) to teach that despite the great joy of the Torah, our gladness remains incomplete without the ultimate rest of a Yom Tov, because \"we are still the servants of Ahasuerus\" (Megillah 14b) and the fasts of Tisha B'Av and the Seventeenth of Tammuz have not yet been uprooted. From Pharaoh's bondage Israel was completely redeemed, for their souls became free through the Torah; but the subjugation to the unholy empire of Ahasuerus persists as long as we dwell in exile under secular monarchs. During the Second Temple, most of Israel remained in the diaspora; had all ascended en masse, the redemption would have been permanent like silver that never rots. Rebbe bathed on the Seventeenth of Tammuz to lighten the burden of exile, and sought to uproot Tisha B'Av when it coincided with Shabbat by drawing upon the Sabbath's holiness to turn it into gladness, though the Sages did not concede because the appointed End had not yet arrived. Rebbe's joyful planting on Purim symbolized the gathering of disciples around Torah (Ta'anit 7a), demonstrating that the greatness of Torah study is revealed specifically when performed from within the darkness of exile and worldly labor!"

                  "text": "Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 3: ‘Our sages, of blessed memory, stated that the Holy One, blessed be He, did not write in the Torah “For the sake of these words,” or “because of these,” or “on account of these words,” but simply according to the tenor of (al pi) these words. This statement clearly alludes to the Oral Law (torah she be-’al peh), which is difficult to learn and in the learning of which there is considerable anguish, comparable to darkness itself, as it is said: The people that walk in darkness have seen a great light (Isa. 9:1). The people referred to in this verse are the masters of the Talmud, who beheld a great light when the Holy One, blessed be He, enlightened them as to what is prohibited and permitted, pure and impure. It is said of them that They that love Him shall be as the sun when it goeth forth in its might (Judg. 5:31).’",

          "h": "The theme: The Megillah recounting Ahasuerus's might as the surrounding husk, and the poverty of the Men of the Great Assembly. The Megillah recounts the might of Ahasuerus because his unholy empire mimics King Solomon’s holy monarchy like an ape before man. Ahasuerus sought to sit upon the throne of Hashem and boasted of his banquet, challenging whether such bliss exists in the World to Come (Esther Rabbah 2:4), imagining his rule was the Kingdom of Heaven in wisdom, might, and riches. In truth, he was merely the unholy husk encasing the fruit—the Men of the Great Assembly who were under his dominion. They embodied the true lower wisdom of Solomon; true might in subduing the yetzer, where they bound the inclination for idolatry and gouged out the eyes of the inclination for licentiousness (Yoma 69b); and true wealth, being content with their lot. Although they enjoyed peace in Babylonia and Persia (wherefore the majority refused to ascend to the Holy Land where poverty was severe, constructing a menorah of wood, Ribash §153), they joyfully chose dry bread in the Land of Israel over all the luxuries of the diaspora. They were worthy of the final redemption, matching the generation of Hezekiah who was considered for Mashiach (Sanhedrin 94a), neither requiring the bow of war (Bereishis Rabbah 35:2); yet sin delayed it, the unholy husk preceding the fruit like darkness preceding light (Shabbat 77b). At the end of the Megillah, even after Esther put on royalty, Ahasuerus laid a tax tribute (Esther 10:1) to mimic King Solomon who imposed levies (I Melachim 9:15), demonstrating that while the salvation was immense, Israel remained under imperial tribute."

          "h": "The theme: The Megillah opening with the chronicle of servitude, light shining from within darkness, and the drunken serenity of Purim. In its literal sense, recounting Ahasuerus's might at the beginning and end was necessary out of dread of the empire, for Israel remained subjects under Persian rule. When the Sages initially hesitated to record the Megillah, arguing: \"You will arouse jealousy and hatred against us among the nations\" (Megillah 7a), Esther answered that the narrative was already inscribed in Persian chronicles. To appease imperial eyes, they recorded the greatness of Ahasuerus. Yet because the Megillah was dictated by the Holy Spirit, it contains no mundane secular history; recounting imperial might is an integral part of the miracle. The Talmud opens the homiletical introduction to Esther with: \"For we are bondmen; yet our God has not forsaken us in our bondage\" (Ezra 9:9; Megillah 11a), teaching that although we are still subjects of Ahasuerus, Hashem never abandoned us. \"When I sit in darkness, Hashem shall be a light unto me\" (Michah 7:8)—Israel toiling in Torah under foreign dominion, which is superior to study in tranquility (Yoma 9b). Wisdom was fully rectified in Israel, whereas among the nations wisdom vanished from Edom (Ovadiah 1:8). But regarding wealth, honor, and might, rectification was achieved only temporarily on Purim as a day of \"feasting and gladness,\" where joy is experienced not through the holiness of the day as on a Yom Tov, but through the banquet of kings in worldly ease. Therefore one must drink ad d'lo yada, attaining mental composure through wine. Through this mitzvah, even mundane serenity is sanctified; one who has a legal dispute with a gentile should schedule it in Adar (Ta'anit 29b), for then Israel’s might dominates worldly foes. In Adar the fear of the Jews fell upon the nations, demonstrating that we are no longer servants of Ahasuerus, serving as the direct prelude to the ultimate redemption of Nisan, linking redemption to redemption!"

          "h": "The theme: Shavuot as the season of the Giving of the Torah (Zman Matan Torateinu), the prayer established by the Men of the Great Assembly, and the calendar dilemma. The core essence of the festival of Shavuot is that it is the season of the Giving of the Torah (Zman Matan Torateinu), as codified by the Men of the Great Assembly in the liturgy (Berachos 33a). One must wonder at the Magen Avraham (Orach Chaim 494:1), who cited Rambam’s wording attributing this title to our custom (minhageinu). In truth, it is an ancient, universally received liturgical foundation instituted by the Great Assembly, for every festival is designated upon the historical divine event wrought within it. The commentators struggled with Rabbi Yose’s talmudic position that the Torah was given on the seventh of Sivan (Shabbat 86b), as well as the calendar fact that according to all opinions the Giving of the Torah took place on the fifty-first day from the Omer offering. Attempting to resolve this by stating that the liturgy alludes to the second diaspora day of the festival is unsatisfactory, for in the Land of Israel only a single day is observed, which is the primary biblical commandment. How could the Torah establish the festival on the fiftieth day if the Giving of the Torah occurred on the fifty-first?"

          "h": "The theme: The fifty days of the Omer, the nocturnal flash of the Exodus versus the permanent acquisition of Sinai, and the double Sabbath. Scripture commands: \"seven weeks shall there be complete; even unto the morrow after the seventh week shall you number fifty days\" (Vayikra 23:15–16). Commentators questioned why the verse says \"number fifty days\" when only forty-nine are counted. The Zohar (III, 97a) compares the Omer counting to a woman counting her seven clean days, purifying the seven emotional traits (Middot), each comprising seven (49 days), with the fiftieth day corresponding to the understanding of the heart (Binah) whence all attributes flow. At the Exodus, the divine illumination descended in an unearned flash (\"skipping over the mountains\", Shir HaShirim 2:8; Shir HaShirim Rabbah): Hashem passed through Egypt in His glory, dispelling all darkness from their hearts. Yet that revelation was temporary, vanishing to require active human toil. The residual impression (reshimu) remained, enabling Israel through the forty-nine days of the Omer to re-acquire that light permanently, until at Sinai the Torah was given as an eternal gift (Matan Torah). Scripture designates the first day of Pesach \"Shabbat\" (\"on the morrow after the Shabbat\", Vayikra 23:15) because Shabbat represents an immutable holiness descending directly from Hashem without prior human effort, whereas a Yom Tov is sanctified through human initiative (Yisrael d'kadshinhu). The Omer counts forty-nine days to reach that lofty Sabbath-light of Pesach, with the fiftieth day being the culmination of all effort. One toils and then discovers the gift like a lost treasure found unexpectedly (yagati u-matzati, Megillah 6b; Sanhedrin 97a). In Creation, Hashem worked for six days and rested on the seventh; but Adam was created on Friday and entered Shabbat immediately, receiving an initial divine awakening (itaruta d'le'ila) before engaging in secular work. This is the mystery of the two Sabbaths (Shabbat 118b): Moshe received the commandment of Shabbat in the Manna on Sunday, but withheld telling Israel until Friday (Shemos 16:5; Bava Kamma 92a) because he knew Israel could not attain the holiness of Shabbat through their own effort until they had first experienced it as an unearned divine gift!"

        {
          "h": "The theme: The two letters Hei as the upper and lower Sabbaths, the portal of freedom (Tar'a d'Cheiru), and the three Sabbaths of Marah. The two letters Hei of the Name Havayah embody two Sabbaths: from Hashem's vantage from above to below, the Supernal Sabbath (Binah / the upper Hei) precedes the six workdays, while the Lower Sabbath (Malkhut / the lower Hei) follows them. But from Israel's ascending perspective from below to above, it is reversed: Israel first grasps the Lower Sabbath where Hashem dwells amidst their defilement, and through their striving ascends to the Supernal Sabbath in the understanding of the heart (Binah), where a pure heart is created. This is the Great Sabbath (Shabbat HaGadol), the Portal of Freedom (Tar'a d'Cheiru) of the Jubilee (Yovel) arriving after seven sabbatical cycles. At Pesach the Shechinah descended into Egypt amidst defilement; through the seven weeks of the Omer Israel purified their seven emotional attributes, meriting at Sinai the Portal of Freedom where no sin offering (chatat) is brought on Shavuot, for they were cleansed of sin. In every Sabbath there are two lights: the light of the Moon (the night of Shabbat) and the light of the Sun (the day of Shabbat), encompassed in the three Sabbath meals. At Marah before the Manna, Israel observed three Sabbaths (the Exodus having occurred on Thursday, crossing the Sea on Wednesday, and arriving at Marah over Thursday, Friday, and Shabbat, Shabbat 87b). Tosafos questioned how Israel could have desecrated their first Sabbath if they were already commanded at Marah. At Marah they received the immutable Sabbath descending directly from Hashem (k'vi'a v'kayma); in the Manna they experienced the Sabbath achieved through human preparation (hachanah), which guarantees that no foreign nation can dominate them. On that Sabbath they were commanded in Sabbath delight (Oneg Shabbat), the three meals, and received the gift of Shabbat. The final Sabbath of their Omer counting was the Sabbath of Sinai, where the Sabbath was engraved upon the Tablets as an eternal covenant, reaching the Portal of Freedom of the Supernal Sabbath!"

          "h": "The theme: The seven rungs of Shabbat matching the seven biblical festivals, and Yom Kippur as the all-encompassing Shabbat Shabbaton. There are seven rungs within Shabbat itself, each dividing into two (12 aspects) plus their encompassing attributes, and a seventh overarching rung encompassing all six. Corresponding to these seven rungs stand the seven festival days ordained in the Torah that Israel sanctifies: the first and seventh days of Pesach, Shavuot, the first and eighth days of Succos (Shemini Atzeret), Rosh Hashanah, and Yom Kippur. These festivals are likewise designated \"Shabbat\" through the sanctity of Israel. The first and seventh days of Pesach correspond to the two lower aspects of the first Sabbath, with Shavuot unifying them. The first day of Succos and Shemini Atzeret correspond to the two rungs of the second Sabbath achieved through preparation (rejoicing in gathering the harvest of the year), with Rosh Hashanah (the head of the coming year) unifying them. Yom Kippur is the Shabbat Shabbaton encompassing all seven, on which the Second Tablets were given—completing the Giving of the Torah and establishing the indelible engraving of freedom (cheirut) upon the Tablets so that no future sin can ever void it, for \"on this day shall atonement be made for you\" (Vayikra 16:30). Yom Kippur resembles the World to Come, being devoid of eating and drinking (Berachos 17a), rooted in the rung of Binah where repentance and cosmic forgiveness reside: \"and his heart understand, and turn, and be healed\" (Yeshayah 6:10)!"

        {
          "h": "The theme: The Splitting of the Sea standing for the first Sabbath of Chesed, the missing Sabbath of Gevurah, and adding the fifty-first day. During the Omer counting, seven Sabbaths must anchor the seven emotional attributes in the heart. In the wilderness prior to Sinai, there were only five Sabbaths. The seventh day of Pesach (the Splitting of the Sea) stood in place of the first Sabbath of Chesed: the Zohar (II, 48a) teaches that the Splitting of the Sea depended on Atika (the Ancient Holy One), which transcends human striving. At the Sea, Hashem fought for them (\"Hashem shall fight for you, and you shall hold your peace\", Shemos 14:14), acting like the immutable Sabbath (k'vi'a v'kayma) of Chesed. This completed the liberation from Egypt, severing the residual tie with Egypt’s unholy lusts. Yet there still lacked a Sabbath for the attribute of Gevurah—the primary vessel for the Giving of the Torah, which issued from the side of Gevurah (Zohar III, 80b). Therefore, their preparation for the fiftieth day was incomplete. To supply this missing preparation, an extra day was added: either through the intercalation of Iyar according to the Rabbis, or the day Moshe added of his own accord according to Rabbi Yose (Shabbat 87a)! The dispute between Rabbi Yose and the Rabbis reflects whether Moshe added the fiftieth day as an individual day of human striving corresponding to the fiftieth gate of Binah, or whether the second day of the seventh week was doubled by intercalating Iyar. According to all opinions, fifty days were counted in the wilderness because human preparation was required on the fiftieth day itself, for the defilement of the Serpent did not cease until the actual Giving of the Torah (Shabbat 146a). For future generations, however, the defilement ceased at Sinai; hence Hashem promised that the seven weeks of the Omer shall be inherently \"complete\" (temimot), the fiftieth day being included automatically within the forty-nine counted days. Thus Shavuot is eternally celebrated on the anniversary of the Giving of the Torah!"
